content.title: Interesting idea, not corresponding title/focus
content.review:
The main goal of this paper is to learn a ConvNet classifier which performs better for classes in the tail of the class occurrence distribution, ie for classes with relatively few annotated examples. In order to do so, they constrain the final softmax layer, using weights and biases based on the class means, in a nearest-class-mean style layer. In practice the class means are "learned", yet regularised towards the batch class means.

My main concern with the paper is in the theoretical underpinning of the work. From the title a Bayesian approach is suggested, while in practice a rather standard softmax classifier is learned, albeit with a different regulariser (last layer is regularised towards batch class means). Also the Gaussian Mixture Model, is not a true mixture model, in the sense that normally GMMs are used for describing a distribution of unlabelled data, in this case, each class is described with a "Gaussian", and thus the class probabilities are the reseponsibilities proportional to the class Gaussian. To take this one further, it is assumed that there is equal class probabilities and each class has a the same Identity matrix as covariance matrix. Taking away a large part of the Gaussian distribution. The relation (Eq 6) with Softmax is insightful, yet already discussed in eg Mensink et al 2013 (already cited for the Nearest Class Mean classifier). 

A second concern is the experimental exploration. First of all, it is unclear if the method works much better for the tail than the standard softmax. That is not apparent from the results. For example, Fig 4 shows -except for CIFAR10- not a clear relation between class index and proposed relative improvement, it is also unclear if there is just a difficult class (eg at index 150), or that the experiment has been repeated several times. Moreover, when the performance becomes more stable for the classes in the tail, I'd have expected that the standard deviation of the mean class accuracy would decrease, from the results there is no difference between Softmax and the proposed method: 44 +/-1 for Softmax (miniImageNet) to 41 +/-1 for the proposed NCM approach. In the final experiment is the regularised version  compared to an unregularised one, which shows that the first performs better. However, I'm a little unsure about these conclusions, what is the unregularized version exactly doing, how is it different from a standard softmax?

Remaining (minor) remarks:
- It is unclear how iCaRL has been used - it has been proposed as an iterative classification method.
- Eq 2: how would this perform on a learned Softmax representation? Preferably including the (co)variance and class priors?
- Figure 4: Gain -> Relative performance
- The batch size must have a great influence on the functioning of the regularisation (especially when there are many classes, in that case just a single example counts for the class mean). This is not explored in the paper.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Responses to your concerns
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and your feedback. Below are our responses to your concerns:

Approach: As we replied to R1, we aimed to devise a simple solution to the long-tail problem because simple formulations tend to be adopted more frequently than elaborate ones. We agree that more parameters (e.g., priors and covariances) may potentially help, but also increase complexity and limit scalability. Our initial experiments suggest that adding such parameters does not help. In regards to the comment about the Eq. 6, we decided to include the relationship of the nearest-class-mean for completeness. We will add references to the discussion of Mensink et al. 2013 about this relationship in a final version.

Experiments: To highlight the benefits of the proposed method, we added a new experiment that measures the relative performance of classes in the tail and in the head separately. In these experiments (shown in Table 1 in the latest version of the paper), we can observe that the performance of the proposed approach increases the relative performance for classes in the tail and maintains a similar performance for classes in the head in comparison with the softmax classifier. In regards to the experiment measuring the effect of the proposed regularizer, the unregularized unregularized method is equivalent to a Softmax classifier with restricted biases. Specifically, these biases are set to half of the squared norm of the class-centroids, i.e., b = -½ || u_j ||^2. These biases are set to these values according to the Eq. 6 in Section 3.2.

Answers to the minor remarks:
- iCaRl implementation:  iCaRL was not used in an incremental fashion. We computed the deep features from a trained network and calculated the centroids for every class. We will clarify this in a final version.
- Eq 2. How would this perform using softmax representation? iCaRL with unnormalized vectors is equivalent to an isotropic GMM fit to an embedding learned with softmax. Our experiments show that our model generally outperforms such an approach. We are working on fitting a full GMM using softmax features, once we get results we will upload a new version of the submission.
- Gain -> Relative Performance: We have adopted the suggestion in the latest version of the paper.

display_title: Interesting idea. Not sure about novelty and depth of experiments.

content.title: Interesting idea. Not sure about novelty and depth of experiments.
content.review:
The paper aims to address a common issue in many classification applications: that the number of training data from different classes is much unbalanced. The paper proposes a Bayesian framework to address it with a Gaussian mixture model.

Overall the math looks reasonable. I am not sure about the novelty of the paper, as it is a relatively standard definition of Bayesian math. Essentially, instead of computing a softmax prediction which is the discrimination probability of each class given the input, one uses a logistic regression type interpretation (equation 1). This has been used in multi-class classification before. For example, many early SVM papers deal with multi-class classification by training 1-vs-all classifiers on each class and then choose the one having the highest score (possibly with a class-prior adjustment).

Note that this actually changes the underlying assumption a bit: softmax basically assumes the classes are mutually exclusive, while this interpretation implicitly assumes that the classes are not related to each other - an image could belong to multiple classes. This probably does not match the assumption of many of the datasets being tested upon (CIFAR, MNIST) but I don't consider that a fundamental issue.

I am quite a bit concerned about the experimentation protocol as well. The datasets are relatively smaller scale, and datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR are known to overfit. As a result, although there are approaches taken to generate unbalanced datasets out of them (e.g. MNIST). Regardless, the results seem to suggest that the proposed method is similar to softmax performance - which is expected as they are similar - but I am not sure if it accurately evaluated / analyzed the possible application and performance gain of the proposed method.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Responses to your concerns
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and your feedback. Below are our responses to your concerns:

Novelty of approach: From a theoretical perspective, we introduce a deep Bayesian class-conditional Gaussian model that explicitly factors out class imbalances for long-tailed learning. From a practical perspective, our final approach (Eq. 5) is similar to softmax learning but differs in its use of a restricted bias term, and more importantly, an additional regularization term that forces the softmax weights to lie close to class centroids. As Fig. 5 shows, this regularizer noticeably improves performance. Finally, our underlying generative model (Eq. 1) assumes that data is generated from a single class, and so we don’t understand the reviewer’s comment about “multiple classes.”

Evaluation: We are currently working on getting larger and naturally long-tailed datasets. Once we get results on these, we will upload a new version of the paper. We added a new experiment that measures the relative performance of classes in the tail and in the head separately. In these experiments (see Table 1 in the latest version of the paper), we can observe that the performance of the proposed approach increases the relative performance for classes in the tail and maintains a similar performance for classes in the head in comparison with a softmax classifier. Recall that the relative performance is computed as the ratio of the per-class accuracy of the proposed method and the accuracy of the softmax classifier.

content.title: No Title
content.review:
This paper presents a method based on a Bayesian classifier that improves classification of rare classes in datasets with long tail class distributions. The method is based on balance the class-priors to generalize well for rare classes. By using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), authors are able to obtain a factorization of class-likelihoods and class-priors leading to a closed-form maximum likelihood estimation that can be integrated to differente classification models, such as current deep learning classifiers. Authors, also propose an evaluation approach that addresses the bias towards the head and intra-class-variation of classes in the tail.

They face class imbalance problems, particular long tail distributions, by fixing: i) The covariance matrices of all the classes to be the identity, and ii) The priors over each class to be uniform. So all classes, popular and rare, have equal weight for Bayesian classification. To me, this is not a fundamental way to solve the long-tail problem, in the sense that by fixing isotropic likelihoods and flat priors, authors are also ignoring information that can be relevant in some classification problems, where a good prior can be useful to disambiguate confusing situations. On other hand, using a unimodal function to model each class is an over-simplification that ignores intra-class complexity. 

The datasets used by the authors are balanced, so they artificially transform them into long-tailed, it will be good to test directly on real long-tailed datasets. The experimentation is only performed using small to medium datasets (< 80K instances), it will be good to show if the benefits of the proposed approach can also be present in the case of large datasets. In this sense, I agree with the authors that the evaluation protocol for long-tailed datasets can't be just based on average accuracy, however, the protocol proposed requires to train the model several times, therefore, it does not scale properly to large datasets that are the common rule in the deep learning world. Results respect to similar state-of-the-art techniques shows a reasonable improvement (depends of the dataset, approx. 1-3%).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Responses to your concerns
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and your feedback. Below are our responses to your concerns:

Approach: We aimed to devise a simple solution to the long-tail problem, because simple formulations tend to be adopted more frequently than elaborate ones. We agree that more parameters (e.g., priors and covariances) may help the network to generalize better for long-tailed datasets. However, adding more parameters will significantly increase complexity and decrease scalability of the proposed method. In regards to class-variation, we would agree with the reviewer if we were learning models defined on a fixed feature embedding. But importantly, we are learning a nonlinear embedding *such that* classes can be modeled with a single isotropic Gaussian.

Evaluation: We are currently working on getting larger and naturally long-tailed datasets. Once we get results on these, we will upload a new version of the paper. In regards to the scalability of the proposed evaluation protocol, we prioritized correctness over scalability. We believe that the first step towards a good evaluation protocol for learning from long-tailed datasets is to establish a consistent protocol for measuring performance. We will investigate the development of a more scalable evaluation protocol as the next step of this work. In regards to the results, we added a new experiment that shows that our proposed method consistently provides improvement for classes in the tail w/o sacrificing much performance for classes in the head; please see Table 1 in the new version of the submission.

content.title: New Experiments Implementing Full Priors and Covariances
content.comment: As R1 and R4 requested, we implemented an approach that fits a full GMM approach (i.e., priors and covariances) to the representation learned with plain softmax. The results were added to Fig. 4. This GMM approach did well for classes in the head but fell short for classes in the tail. The reason for this drop in performance is the lack of data to estimate good covariance matrices. This experiment shows that our approach performs better than this GMM approach, and that our formulation performs better than the GMM approach on long-tailed datasets.
